valueChain.summary: E-commerce makes money either by selling products at a gross margin (brands and inventory-led retailers) or by charging a take rate on other people's sales (marketplaces), and then spending much of that margin to acquire customers, deliver orders and handle returns. Profit depends on contribution per order after marketing, shipping and returns, and on how many orders a customer places before they stop buying.

stages.name: Product & sourcing
activities: Contract manufacturing or sourcing from suppliers
Quality testing and labelling compliance (BIS, FSSAI, Legal Metrology)
revenueDrivers: Gross margin set by product cost against selling price
costDrivers: Raw material, component and packaging prices
Minimum order quantities and batch sizes

kpis.name: Gross margin
kpis.formula: (net revenue - cost of goods) / net revenue
kpis.benchmark: Approx. 55-70% for D2C beauty and personal care, 40-55% for D2C apparel, 10-20% for electronics resellers

stages.marginNote: Brands earn high gross margins (often 50%+) but hand most of it to later stages; contract manufacturers earn approx. 8-15% EBITDA.

stages.name: Demand generation
activities: Performance marketing on social and search
revenueDrivers: Volume and quality (purchase intent) of traffic sent to the storefront
costDrivers: Cost per click or impression, which rises in festive season

kpis.name: Customer acquisition cost (CAC)
kpis.benchmark: Approx. ₹300-1,000 for Indian D2C brands, depending on category and price point

kpis.name: Return on ad spend (ROAS)
kpis.formula: revenue attributed to ads / ad spend
kpis.benchmark: Approx. 2.5-4x is a common D2C target on first purchase

stages.marginNote: Ad platforms earn very high margins; for a young D2C brand marketing is usually the largest cost after product (approx. 20-35% of revenue).

stages.name: Storefront & conversion
activities: Marketplace listings or own website and app
Checkout and prepaid payments (UPI, cards, wallets, pay later)
costDrivers: Marketplace commission and fees (approx. 15-35% of selling price including fees)
Payment gateway fees (approx. 1.5-2% on cards; UPI has no merchant discount rate on payments up to ₹2,000 and about 0.4% above that from 15 October 2026, and some gateways add platform fees)

kpis.name: Take rate
kpis.benchmark: Approx. 15-30% for large Indian marketplaces including fees and ads

stages.marginNote: Scaled marketplaces with strong advertising income capture the largest profit pool; brand websites avoid commission but must pay for all their traffic.

stages.name: Warehousing & fulfilment
revenueDrivers: Fulfilment and storage fees (for marketplaces and 3PLs)
costDrivers: Inventory holding cost and write-offs of ageing stock

kpis.name: Order accuracy
kpis.formula: orders shipped without error / orders shipped

stages.marginNote: Thin for 3PLs (approx. 5-10% EBITDA); for a brand it is a cost of approx. ₹30-80 per order plus the cash tied up in stock.

stages.name: Shipping & last-mile delivery
activities: Cash collection and remittance for COD orders
revenueDrivers: Shipping fees charged to brands and buyers
costDrivers: Rider pay per drop and drop density

kpis.name: Cost per shipment
kpis.benchmark: Approx. ₹50-90 for a standard parcel within India

kpis.name: First-attempt delivery rate
kpis.formula: orders delivered on first attempt / orders attempted
kpis.benchmark: Approx. 85-90% for prepaid orders, lower for COD

stages.marginNote: Low-margin, scale-driven business (approx. 2-8% EBITDA for parcel companies); delivery density decides profitability.

stages.name: Returns, service & retention
activities: Inspection, grading and resale of returned stock
Customer support, CRM messages, loyalty and subscriptions

kpis.name: Return rate
kpis.formula: orders returned by customers / orders delivered
kpis.benchmark: Approx. 25-35% in online fashion; under 10% in beauty and most electronics

kpis.name: RTO rate
kpis.benchmark: Approx. 20-30% for COD orders against 2-5% for prepaid

kpis.name: 12-month repeat rate
kpis.formula: customers buying again within 12 months / customers acquired

stages.marginNote: Mostly a cost centre, but retention is where D2C profit is made: repeat orders carry little or no acquisition cost.

valueChain.profitPools: Most profit goes to the players that own customer traffic: scaled marketplaces (take rates of approx. 15-30% plus high-margin advertising) and the ad platforms. Brands earn good margins only when repeat purchase and own-website share are high, because the gross margin they make at sourcing is otherwise spent on acquisition and channel fees. Warehousing and logistics are scale businesses with thin margins.

unitEconomics.unit: per order, Indian D2C personal care brand selling on its own website (approx.)

lines.item: Average order value (net of discounts and GST)
Marketing per order (acquisition spend spread over orders)
Returns and RTO cost (allocated per order)

unitEconomics.result: Contribution after marketing ≈ ₹240 per order (20% of order value), before salaries, rent and technology

valueChain.india: Foreign direct investment rules shape the industry: foreign-owned firms may sell to Indian consumers only as marketplaces, cannot own the inventory sold on them, and cannot let sellers in which they or their group hold equity sell on their platform (Press Note 2 of 2018); since Press Note 3 of 2026 (July 2026) they may also hold inventory, but only to export goods made in India. Domestic retailers and D2C brands can hold stock. Cash on delivery is still common outside the metros and drives high RTO rates, even as UPI has made prepaid payment easier, and quick commerce has become a major channel for everyday goods in the metros.

workedExample.problem: A D2C brand's contribution margin fell about 6 points in a year even though order value, product cost and cost per click were flat.
trace: Storefront (s3) and sourcing (s1) look clean: conversion, order value, discounts and gross margin are unchanged, so the cause is elsewhere in the chain.
Demand generation (s2): the brand shifted ad spend to tier 2 and 3 audiences, and the share of orders paid by COD rose from 30% to 70%.
Shipping (s5): COD orders are refused or undeliverable 28% of the time against 4% for prepaid, so the blended RTO rate rose from 11% to 21% of shipped orders.

Returns (s6) and marketing per delivered order: each RTO costs about ₹210 in two-way shipping and repacking, so RTO cost per delivered order rose from ₹26 to ₹55, and marketing per delivered order rose from ₹338 to ₹379 because the same spend now produces fewer delivered orders.
Together that is about ₹70 per delivered order, roughly 6 points on a ₹1,200 order: the root cause is audience targeting in s2, which shows up as cost in s5 and s6.
workedExample.lesson: In Indian D2C the quality of a growth channel shows up two stages later, so judge acquisition on cost per delivered (and kept) order, not per order placed.

cases.title: Skincare brand growing but losing money
cases.prompt: Our client is a Mumbai-based D2C skincare brand that sells through its own website, online marketplaces and, since last year, quick commerce apps. Revenue grew 40% to ₹180 crore last year, but EBITDA margin swung from +4% to -6%. The founders want to understand why they are losing money while growing so fast.
clarifyingFacts: Q: What is the objective? A: Find the causes of the margin fall and get back to breakeven within 12 months.
Q: How is revenue split by channel? A: Own website 45% (down from 60%), marketplaces 40%, quick commerce 15% (new this year).
Q: Have prices changed? A: List prices are unchanged, but the average discount rose from 18% to 24% because of more marketplace sale events.
Q: What happened to marketing? A: Marketing rose from 28% to 34% of revenue as the brand pushed into tier 2 cities through paid social ads.

modelTree.label: Why did EBITDA margin fall from +4% to -6% despite 40% growth?

children.label: Deeper discounts during marketplace sale events
Mix shift to lower-priced minis and trial kits
Expiry write-offs from stock spread across new channels
Higher cost per click on tier 2 paid social
Fewer repeat orders to spread acquisition spend over
Channel fees: marketplace commission and quick commerce margins
Fulfilment, shipping, payment and returns cost
Salaries: team hired ahead of scale

hypotheses: Deeper discounts (18% to 24% of list price) cut net revenue per unit by about 7%; with product, shipping and fulfilment (costs that do not fall with price) at roughly half of revenue, this alone explains about 4 of the 10 points lost.
Marketing rising from 28% to 34% of revenue reflects higher acquisition cost in tier 2 paid social that repeat purchases have not yet paid back.
Channel fees are rising mechanically as the own-website share fell from 60% to 45%, since marketplace and quick commerce fees take roughly 25-35% of selling price.
hints: Use the profit equation, but express it per order and separate costs that move with each order from those that do not.
First-level branches: net revenue per order fell; variable cost per order rose; overheads grew faster than revenue.
Net revenue per order: deeper discounts in marketplace sale events; mix shift to lower-priced minis and trial kits; fewer units per order.

keyMetrics.name: Contribution per order
keyMetrics.formula: net revenue per order - product cost - channel fees - fulfilment, shipping and payment cost - returns cost - marketing per order

keyMetrics.name: EBITDA margin
keyMetrics.formula: (total contribution - overheads) / net revenue

commonMistakes: Treating 40% revenue growth as a sign of health instead of checking contribution per order by channel.
Lumping channel fees into a generic 'costs' bucket, which hides that they rise automatically as sales move from the own website to marketplaces and quick commerce.

frameworkPick.why: The question is why margin fell while revenue rose, which is a diagnosis of revenue and cost drivers: exactly what a profitability tree is built for.

distractorWhyNot.growth: The client is already growing fast; the problem is the quality of that growth, not how to get more of it.
distractorWhyNot.pricing: Discounting is one likely cause, but a pricing tree would leave out marketing, channel fees and overheads.
distractorWhyNot.turnaround: There is no cash crisis or lender deadline; the first job is to diagnose which revenue and cost drivers moved, which a profitability tree does.

cases.title: Online pet food market in India
cases.prompt: A venture-backed D2C pet care start-up is preparing its fundraising deck and wants a credible number for the size of India's online pet food market today. A rival's deck quotes about ₹6,000 crore, which the founders suspect is too high. How big is the online market in rupees per year?
clarifyingFacts: Q: Which pets should I include? A: Dogs and cats; other pets are under 5% of pet food spend and can be ignored.
Q: Does home-cooked food count? A: No, only packaged food: dry food, wet food and treats.
Q: What can I assume about pet numbers? A: About 3 crore pet dogs and 50 lakh pet cats; about 30% of dogs and 35% of cats eat packaged food regularly.

Q: What about spend and channel? A: Packaged food spend averages about ₹500 a month per dog and ₹400 per cat; online channels (marketplaces, quick commerce, brand websites) take about 30% of packaged pet food sales.

modelTree.label: Annual online sales of packaged dog and cat food in India (₹)

children.label: Share of dogs fed packaged food (about 30%)
Annual packaged food spend per dog
Share of that spend made online
Share of cats fed packaged food (about 35%)
Annual packaged food spend per cat
Share of that spend made online

hypotheses: Dogs are about 87% of the market because there are six times as many pet dogs as cats and each spends more.
The total packaged market is about ₹6,240 crore, so the rival's ₹6,000 crore is the whole packaged market; the online market is about 30% of it, roughly ₹1,900 crore a year.
The share of dogs fed packaged food is the most sensitive assumption: moving it 10 points (30% to 40%) changes the answer by nearly 30%.
hints: Segment first by the factor that changes both the number of buyers and the spend per buyer, then build each segment as a chain of multiplied drivers.
First-level branches: online dog food sales; online cat food sales (other pets are under 5% and excluded by the interviewer).
Cat branch: number of pet cats x share fed packaged food x annual spend per cat x share bought online.

keyMetrics.name: Online dog food market
keyMetrics.formula: pet dogs x % fed packaged food x annual spend per dog x online share

keyMetrics.name: Online pet food market
keyMetrics.formula: online dog food market + online cat food market

commonMistakes: Forgetting to apply the online share, so the answer given is the whole packaged pet food market rather than the online part.
Applying one ownership rate to all ~30 crore Indian households, which ignores that packaged food use is concentrated in urban, higher-income homes.

frameworkPick.why: The client asks how big the market is, an estimation question answered by multiplying population, penetration, spend and channel share.

distractorWhyNot.pe-dd: Investors will diligence the company later, but the question asks only for the market number, not whether to invest.
distractorWhyNot.segmentation: Splitting by pet type is a step in the estimate, but the question is not which segment to target.
distractorWhyNot.growth: The question is today's market size, not how to grow the start-up's revenue.

cases.title: Should a D2C brand charge for COD?
cases.prompt: A D2C footwear brand gets about 1 lakh orders a month on its website, 60% of them cash on delivery (COD). About 25% of COD orders are refused or undeliverable and come back (RTO), against 4% of prepaid orders. The founder is considering a ₹49 fee on COD orders. Should she introduce it?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What does an RTO cost? A: About ₹180 per order in two-way shipping and repacking; the shoes go back into stock.
Q: What does a delivered order earn? A: Average order value ₹1,500 at 55% gross margin; forward shipping ₹80; COD handling ₹40 per delivered COD order, against a 2% gateway fee on prepaid orders.

Q: How will customers react? A: A small test suggests 30% of COD buyers would switch to prepaid (with an RTO rate of about 6%), 8% would abandon, and RTO on the remaining COD orders would fall from 25% to 18%.
Q: What do competitors do? A: Most peers still offer free COD; two have started charging ₹29 to ₹49.

modelTree.label: Should the brand charge ₹49 on COD orders?

children.label: Short-term contribution from today's COD orders
Lower RTO as the fee deters casual orders
Gateway fee in place of COD handling
Contribution lost on orders that would have delivered
RTO cost avoided on orders that would have failed
Repeat purchase by tier 2 and 3 COD customers
Fee level and exemptions, e.g. waived for repeat buyers
Clear disclosure of the fee before checkout

hypotheses: On the test figures the fee adds about ₹0.47 crore of contribution a month, mostly from RTO savings rather than fee income.
The fee stays worthwhile unless more than about 21% of COD buyers abandon (with 30% switching to prepaid), well above the 8% seen in the test.
Abandonment will be highest among first-time tier 3 buyers, whose COD orders have the highest RTO, so the orders lost are worth less than average.
hints: Group today's COD buyers by how they will respond to the fee, and keep this month's economics separate from effects that build over time.
First-level branches: short-term contribution from today's COD orders; longer-term customer impact; fee design and execution.
Longer-term customer impact: checkout conversion of first-time visitors; repeat purchase by tier 2 and 3 COD customers.

keyMetrics.name: Contribution per COD order placed
keyMetrics.formula: (1 - RTO rate) x (gross margin - shipping - COD handling + fee) - RTO rate x RTO cost

keyMetrics.name: Blended RTO rate
keyMetrics.formula: orders returned undelivered / orders shipped

commonMistakes: Counting only the ₹49 fee income and missing that the larger gain is fewer RTOs from buyers who switch or drop out.
Treating every abandoned order as a full lost sale, when about a quarter of them would have come back undelivered anyway.

frameworkPick.why: It is a decision on whether to charge a new fee, so the tree weighs how customers respond (stay, switch, abandon) against fee income and cost savings.

distractorWhyNot.profitability: No profit fall is being diagnosed; the question is the effect of one specific price change.
distractorWhyNot.operations: Lower RTO is an outcome, but the lever being judged is a price, not a process change.
distractorWhyNot.segmentation: Customer groups appear in the analysis, but the question is not which segment to target.

cases.title: Doubling a men's grooming brand
cases.prompt: Our client is a D2C men's grooming brand with ₹60 crore revenue, 70% of it from beard and hair products sold on its own website and marketplaces. The new CEO wants to double revenue to ₹120 crore in three years without losing money. How could the brand get there?
clarifyingFacts: Q: Is profit a constraint? A: Yes, the brand must stay EBITDA positive (currently 5%), so it cannot buy growth with heavy discounts.
Q: What does the customer base look like? A: About 6 lakh customers bought last year; 30% bought more than once; average order value is ₹550.
Q: Which channels does it use today? A: Own website 45%, marketplaces 55%; no quick commerce or offline presence.
Q: Where are customers? A: India only, with about 65% of sales from the top 8 metros.

modelTree.label: How can the brand grow revenue from ₹60 crore to ₹120 crore in three years?

children.label: Sell more of the current range to current customers
Raise repeat rate: subscriptions and refill reminders
Raise order value: bundles and larger packs
Sell the current range to new customers
More new customers through current channels
Metros: win share from rival brands
Exports to Gulf markets with large Indian communities
Sell new products to current customers
Sell new products to new customers

hypotheses: Repeat purchase is the cheapest lever: today's 1.8 lakh repeat buyers place about 3.7 orders a year, so moving 60,000 one-time buyers to repeat (30% to 40%) adds about ₹9 crore at today's customer numbers.
Quick commerce could add ₹15-20 crore within three years because grooming refills are frequent, low-ticket metro purchases.
Adjacent categories sold to existing customers will grow faster and more profitably than a women's range, which needs new customers and a new brand position.
hints: Use a products x customers grid, then place channels and geographies inside the right cell.
First-level branches: more of the current range to current customers; current range to new customers; new products to current customers; new products to new customers.
New products to current customers: adjacent men's categories (skincare, fragrance); premium and gifting ranges.

keyMetrics.name: Revenue
keyMetrics.formula: customers x orders per customer x average order value

commonMistakes: Listing growth ideas without sizing them against the ₹60 crore gap, so there is no view of which two or three levers matter most.
Ignoring the EBITDA-positive constraint and proposing discount-led acquisition, or listing 'acquire a brand' as a cell of the grid when it is a way of entering a cell.

frameworkPick.why: The CEO asks how to double revenue, which needs a full map of growth levers across products, customers and channels.

distractorWhyNot.market-entry: Entering a new channel or country is one lever, not the whole question.
distractorWhyNot.product-launch: New products are one lever; the question is overall revenue growth.
distractorWhyNot.profitability: The brand is profitable; profit is a constraint, not the problem to diagnose.

cases.title: Cutting returns cost at a fashion marketplace
cases.prompt: A large Indian online fashion marketplace delivers about 1 crore orders a month. Customers return 25% of delivered orders, and another 12% of shipped orders come back undelivered (RTO). Each return or RTO costs about ₹150 on average in reverse logistics, quality checks and markdowns. Management wants to cut the total cost of returns by a third within a year. How would you approach this?
clarifyingFacts: Q: Why do customers return items? A: Size and fit 45%, looked different from the photos 20%, quality defects 10%, wrong or damaged item 10%, changed their mind 15%.
Q: Why do orders come back undelivered? A: Mostly COD: customer refused or unreachable 70%, address problems 20%, suspected fake orders 10%.

Q: Is the cost the same for every return? A: No. An RTO costs about ₹80 because the parcel comes back unopened and is restocked; a customer return costs about ₹190 including quality checks and markdowns. Sellers bear the markdowns, but they count here.
Q: Any constraints? A: Free 15-day returns are a key reason customers buy, so the policy cannot simply be scrapped.

modelTree.label: How can returns cost (about ₹700 crore a year) fall by a third?

children.label: Brand-specific size charts and fit recommendations
Flag customers ordering several sizes to try
Product looked different from the listing
Photo and description standards for sellers
Seller penalties linked to return rates
Quality defects, wrong or damaged items
Exchange or store credit instead of refund
Shorter window for low-value, high-return categories
Order confirmation by call or WhatsApp
Prepaid incentives in high-RTO pin codes
Address errors and failed delivery attempts
Batched pickups in dense pin codes
Processing and quality-check cost at the warehouse
Faster restocking to resell at full price

hypotheses: Customer returns are about 81% of the cost (25 lakh a month at ₹190 against 13.6 lakh RTOs at ₹80), so the target cannot come from RTO alone: removing every RTO would save only about ₹131 crore of the ₹234 crore needed.
Size and fit drive 45% of customer returns; fit tools that cut those by a third would remove 15% of customer returns and save about ₹85 crore a year.
Markdowns from slow restocking are a bigger share of the ₹190 cost of a customer return than reverse shipping, so faster restocking saves more than cheaper pickups.
hints: Write total cost as volume x cost per unit, and notice that the volume comes in two kinds with different causes and different unit costs.
First-level branches: fewer customer returns after delivery; fewer orders returned undelivered (RTO); lower cost per return.
Lower cost per return: reverse pickup cost (batched pickups, drop-off points); processing and quality-check cost; value recovered on returned stock (faster restocking, liquidation).

keyMetrics.name: Total returns cost
keyMetrics.formula: customer returns x ~₹190 + RTOs x ~₹80

keyMetrics.name: Customer return rate
keyMetrics.formula: orders returned by customers / orders delivered

keyMetrics.name: RTO rate
keyMetrics.formula: orders returned undelivered / orders shipped

commonMistakes: Treating RTO and customer returns as one problem at one average cost (₹150), though they have different causes, fixes and unit costs (₹80 against ₹190).
Proposing to scrap free returns, which the client has ruled out and which would cost more in lost conversion than it saves.

frameworkPick.why: The goal is to cut one specific cost by a third, which means working through the volume and unit-cost drivers of the returns process.

distractorWhyNot.profitability: No overall profit fall needs diagnosing; the cost line and target are already defined.
distractorWhyNot.pricing: Return fees are one possible lever, but price is not the core question.
distractorWhyNot.segmentation: Customer groups matter for targeting fixes, but the question is about reducing a process cost.

cases.title: Ethnic-wear brand eyeing the US
cases.prompt: An Indian D2C ethnic-wear brand with ₹250 crore revenue sells almost entirely in India. About 8% of its website traffic already comes from the US, mostly from people of Indian origin, but those visitors convert at a third of the Indian rate. The founders want to know whether to build a dedicated US business and, if so, how.
clarifyingFacts: Q: What is the goal? A: US$10 million of US revenue within three years at a positive contribution margin.
Q: How big is the market? A: Assume about 1.6 million Indian-origin households in the US, each spending about US$300 a year on Indian ethnic wear, mostly for weddings and festivals.
Q: How are US orders handled today? A: Shipped from India through the website; delivery takes 10-14 days and returns are difficult. About 70% of US orders are for a dated event such as a wedding.

Q: What are the order economics? A: Average US order about US$110 at a 55% gross margin. As a case assumption, take total US duty as about 25% of order value: a base apparel duty that varies by fabric, plus the 10% Section 301 duty the US has applied to most Indian goods since July 2026. Low-value parcels no longer enter duty-free: the US$800 de minimis exemption has been suspended since August 2025. Cross-border shipping is about US$15 per order, and a first US order costs about US$35 to acquire.

modelTree.label: Should the brand build a US business aiming for US$10m revenue in three years?

children.label: Is the US diaspora market attractive?
Ethnic-wear spend per household by occasion
Growth: new arrivals, second generation, wedding spend
Other Indian brands shipping from India
Can the brand win customers there?
Current US traffic and repeat buyers
Social media following in the US
Styles and price points for US occasions
Service needs: tailoring, event-date delivery, easy exchanges
Customer acquisition cost and repeat rate
Paid social and search in the US
Upfront investment and time to break even
Ship from India: no inventory risk, slow
US stock point: event-date delivery, inventory risk

hypotheses: US$10 million is only about 2% of a US$480 million diaspora ethnic-wear market, so demand is not the constraint; conversion, delivery speed and returns are.

Shipped from India, a US$110 order leaves about US$18 after product cost (US$49.50), duty (about US$27.50) and shipping (US$15), before returns, so the US$35 acquisition cost is recovered only on the second order: the plan works only with repeat buyers, higher US prices or a US stock point that cuts returns cost.
Most US demand is tied to dated events, so customers who cannot get delivery before a wedding go to local boutiques, which explains the low conversion today.
hints: Use the standard four-question logic of an entry decision, ordered from the outside in.
First-level branches: market attractiveness; ability to win customers; economics; entry model.
Ability to win: brand awareness among US customers; product fit (sizing, styles and price points); service needs (tailoring, event-date delivery, exchanges).

keyMetrics.name: Contribution per US order
keyMetrics.formula: order value - product cost - duty (~25% of declared value) - shipping - returns cost

keyMetrics.name: Required market share
keyMetrics.formula: US$10m / (households x spend per household)

commonMistakes: Sizing the whole US apparel market instead of the diaspora ethnic-wear segment the brand actually sells into.
Jumping to 'open a US warehouse' before checking why current US visitors convert at a third of the Indian rate.

frameworkPick.why: The founders ask whether and how to enter a new country, which calls for testing attractiveness, ability to win, economics and entry mode.

distractorWhyNot.growth: The US is one specific growth option; the question is whether and how to enter it, not all ways to grow.
distractorWhyNot.market-sizing: Market size is one input, but the question asks for an entry decision.
distractorWhyNot.operations: Slow delivery and difficult returns are part of the answer, but the question is whether to build a US business at all, which also needs market, economics and entry mode.

cases.title: Online grocer under quick commerce attack
cases.prompt: Our client is an Indian online grocery company offering scheduled next-day delivery in 8 large cities, with an average order value of about ₹1,300. Since quick commerce apps expanded aggressively, its monthly orders have fallen 18% in a year, though revenue has fallen only 9%. How should it respond?
clarifyingFacts: Q: Which orders were lost? A: A year ago 40% of orders were baskets under ₹600 (average ₹450), 27% were ₹600-2,000 (average ₹1,000) and 33% were stock-up baskets over ₹2,000 (average ₹2,600). Small baskets fell 40%, mid-size 2% and stock-up 5%.
Q: How profitable are the different baskets? A: Contribution is about 6% of revenue on stock-up baskets and negative on small baskets, because delivery costs about ₹90 per order whatever the size.
Q: What are competitors doing? A: Quick commerce apps deliver in 10-20 minutes, now carry around 10,000 items, and are using discounts to push larger baskets.
Q: What are the client's strengths? A: Large city warehouses with 25,000+ items, strong fresh produce sourcing, and a loyal base of families placing weekly orders.

modelTree.label: How should the client respond to quick commerce taking 18% of its orders?

children.label: Where and why is it losing?
Orders and revenue lost by basket size
Which customers: fully lapsed vs ordering less often
Their push into large baskets and fresh produce
Price and range advantage on monthly baskets
Match on speed in selected areas
Own dark stores in dense pin codes
Minimum order value or small-basket fee
Partner with a quick commerce app for top-ups

hypotheses: The client has mostly lost loss-making small top-up baskets, while its profitable stock-up business is largely intact, so copying 10-minute delivery could destroy value.

The real threat is quick commerce moving into large baskets: stock-up baskets are about two-thirds of revenue and most of the contribution, so their 5% fall costs more profit than the 40% fall in small baskets, which probably raised total contribution.
A membership built around weekly family orders and fresh produce defends the profitable core at lower cost than a dark store network.
hints: Order the tree as a sequence from diagnosis to decision, not as a list of tactics.
First-level branches: where and why it is losing; how lasting the threat is; response options; how to choose.
How lasting the threat is: competitors' staying power (their contribution per order, funding runway); their push into large baskets and fresh produce.

keyMetrics.name: Contribution per order by basket size
keyMetrics.formula: basket value x gross margin - delivery cost (~₹90) - picking and packing cost

keyMetrics.name: Average order value
keyMetrics.formula: revenue / orders: 0.91 / 0.82 ≈ +11%, because small baskets were lost

commonMistakes: Assuming the client must copy 10-minute delivery without first checking that the lost orders were small, loss-making baskets.
Ignoring rivals' economics: a competitor burning cash may not sustain its discounts, which changes whether to fight now or wait.

frameworkPick.why: A rival's move has caused the order loss and the client must decide how to react, so the tree starts from the threat and weighs responses.

distractorWhyNot.pricing: Discount gaps are one reason customers switch, but the rival's advantage is mainly speed and range, so the question is how to respond to its whole proposition, not what to charge.
distractorWhyNot.profitability: Profit matters for judging options, but the trigger and question are about a competitor's move.
distractorWhyNot.growth: The immediate task is defending the profitable core, not finding new sources of growth.

cases.title: Launching a diaper subscription
cases.prompt: A D2C baby care brand in India sells diapers and wipes through its website and app to about 4 lakh active customers. Parents use up a diaper pack roughly every three weeks, but only 35% of diaper customers buy from the brand again within 60 days. The brand is considering a subscription with 10% off automatic monthly deliveries. Should it launch, and how should the offer be designed?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What is the objective? A: Raise repeat purchase and lifetime value; the target is for subscriptions to reach 25% of diaper revenue within 18 months.
Q: What are the economics today? A: Average diaper order ₹1,100 at 40% gross margin (₹440); win-back ads cost about ₹60 per repeat order.
Q: Where do lapsed customers go? A: Surveys say most buy from quick commerce apps or marketplaces when they run out before the brand's 2-4 day delivery arrives.
Q: Can payments be automated? A: Yes, through UPI AutoPay and card mandates; about 60% of customers pay by UPI.

modelTree.label: Should the brand launch a 10%-off diaper subscription, and in what form?

children.label: Will parents sign up and stay?
Changing sizes as the baby grows
Alternatives: quick commerce, marketplace deals, local chemists
Cancellation at the move to pull-ups or toilet training
Margin given away on orders that would have happened anyway
Margin gained from customers who would have lapsed
Cost of reschedules and failed payments
How should the offer be designed?
Delivery cadence: fixed monthly or matched to use
UPI AutoPay and card mandate success rates
Delivery before the customer runs out

hypotheses: The subscription pays only if 60-day repeat among subscribers rises from 35% to above about 40%, because the 10% discount (₹110) costs more than the ₹60 win-back ads it replaces.
Most early sign-ups will be parents who already reorder, so the discount may mostly subsidise existing loyal demand unless the offer targets lapsing customers.

Parents use a pack every three weeks, so a monthly plan leaves them about one pack short every three months and sends them to quick commerce; matching the cadence to use, and upgrading sizes automatically, will cut churn more than a deeper discount.
hints: Use the standard launch questions, but make the economics incremental: compare with what customers would have done without the offer.
First-level branches: will parents sign up and stay; does it make money; how should the offer be designed; can the brand deliver it.
Can the brand deliver it: stock forecasting by diaper size; recurring payments (mandate success rates, recovery of failed payments); delivery before the customer runs out.

keyMetrics.name: Incremental margin per subscriber
keyMetrics.formula: subscribed orders x (gross margin - discount) - orders that would have happened anyway x (gross margin - win-back cost)

commonMistakes: Counting every subscription order as extra revenue, when many subscribers would have reordered anyway.
Taking 'monthly' from the brief at face value: with a pack used every three weeks and sizes changing every few months, a rigid monthly plan sends too little, then the wrong size.

frameworkPick.why: The brand is deciding whether to launch a new offer and how to design it, so the tree tests demand, economics, design and delivery.

distractorWhyNot.pricing: The discount is one design choice, but the question is whether to launch the offer at all.
distractorWhyNot.growth: Higher lifetime value is the goal, but the question is about one specific new offer.
distractorWhyNot.operations: Forecasting and delivery are part of the answer, not the whole decision.

cases.title: Who should a paid loyalty programme target?
cases.prompt: An Indian online fashion and lifestyle marketplace has about 2 crore customers who bought in the last year. It plans to launch a paid loyalty programme at ₹299 a year, offering free delivery, early access to sales and faster refunds. Which customer segments should it target first?
clarifyingFacts: Q: What is the objective? A: Grow profitable spend per customer; the programme should at least cover the cost of its benefits in year one.
Q: What do we know about customers? A: The top 10% by spend generate about 45% of sales; about 40% of customers bought only once last year.

Q: What do the benefits cost? A: Free delivery waives a ₹40 fee on orders below the ₹499 free-delivery threshold; contribution after returns averages about ₹60 per order, not counting any delivery fee; early sale access costs little; faster refunds raise fraud and return risk.
Q: How do return rates vary? A: From about 10% for some customers to over 50% for heavy 'buy and try' customers.

modelTree.label: Which customer segments should the ₹299 paid loyalty programme target first?

children.label: Segment customers by order frequency and order value
Value to the marketplace of each segment
Orders per year x order value
Extra spend the programme could unlock
More orders once delivery is free
Fraud and return risk from faster refunds
Appeal of the programme to each segment
Value of benefits against the ₹299 fee
Value placed on early sale access
Willingness to prepay: past use of paid memberships

hypotheses: Test first: frequent, low-value buyers with low return rates. They pay the ₹40 fee most often, so the offer is worth most to them (it pays for itself after about 7.5 sub-threshold orders a year), but it pays for the marketplace only if it changes behaviour: a member who already places 10 fee-paying orders a year costs ₹400 in waived fees against the ₹299 fee, so must add about 2 orders a year at ₹60 contribution to break even.
Frequent, high-value buyers mostly order above the free-delivery threshold already, so the programme gives them little new and adds little spend.
High-return 'buy and try' customers should be excluded from faster refunds, or the programme turns them loss-making.
hints: Define segments on the behaviours that decide whether the benefits change what a customer does, then score each segment from both sides of the deal.
First-level branches: segment customers by frequency and order value; value of each segment to the marketplace; appeal of the programme to each segment.
Appeal to each segment: value of the benefits against the ₹299 fee (delivery fees saved, early sale access); likely sign-up rate.

keyMetrics.name: Customer payback on fee
keyMetrics.formula: ₹299 / delivery fee saved per order (~₹40) ≈ 7.5 orders a year

keyMetrics.name: Incremental contribution per member
keyMetrics.formula: ₹299 fee + extra orders x ~₹60 - ₹40 fees waived on orders that would have paid the fee anyway - extra refund and fraud cost

commonMistakes: Targeting the top 10% of spenders by default, when the question is where the programme changes behaviour, not who spends most.
Ignoring return rates: a high-spend but high-return segment can become loss-making once refunds are faster.

frameworkPick.why: The programme and fee are set; the question is which customer groups to target first, so the tree defines segments and ranks them.

distractorWhyNot.pricing: The fee is fixed at ₹299; the question is who to target, not what to charge.
distractorWhyNot.growth: Higher spend is the aim, but the question asks specifically to choose between customer groups.
distractorWhyNot.product-launch: The launch decision is made; only the target audience is open.

cases.title: PE bet on a supplements brand
cases.prompt: A PE fund is considering buying a 60% stake in an Indian D2C sports nutrition brand. Revenue grew 55% last year to ₹450 crore, EBITDA is -3%, and the founders want a valuation of 4.5 times revenue. The fund targets a 25% IRR over five years. Should it invest at this price?
clarifyingFacts: Q: Where is growth coming from? A: Marketplaces and quick commerce rose from 40% to 62% of revenue in two years; own-website revenue is flat.
Q: What does customer data show? A: New customers doubled, but the share of a yearly cohort still buying after 12 months fell from 32% (FY24 cohort) to 21% (FY25 cohort).
Q: How is the product made? A: Two contract manufacturers make 85% of volume; one received an FSSAI notice last year over label claims, since resolved.
Q: What do comparable deals look like? A: Recent Indian consumer brand deals have been priced at 2-4 times revenue, higher only for profitable brands.

modelTree.label: Should the fund buy 60% at 4.5x revenue (₹2,025 crore value) for a 25% IRR?

children.label: Shift to marketplaces and quick commerce
Who owns the customer and the price
FSSAI rules on nutraceutical labels and claims
Is the business sound and its growth repeatable?
Website vs marketplace vs quick commerce
Share of direct and organic traffic
Expand offline: gyms, chemists, modern trade
Do returns work at this price?
Entry price against comparable deals (2-4x revenue)
About ₹6,180 crore for a 3.05x money multiple
Revenue and margin needed at a realistic exit multiple

hypotheses: Growth is being bought: cohort retention falling from 32% to 21% and the shift to marketplaces mean new revenue is less repeatable and lower-margin than the 55% headline suggests.

At 4.5x revenue the fund needs an exit value of about ₹6,180 crore; if exit multiples settle at 3x, revenue must reach about ₹2,060 crore (36% a year for five years), which weakening retention makes unlikely.
The deal works only at a lower price (nearer 3x revenue) or with part of the price tied to retention and EBITDA milestones.
hints: Use the standard due diligence sequence, but let the cohort and channel data decide where you go deepest.
First-level branches: market attractiveness; soundness and repeatability of growth; value the fund can create; returns at this price.

Market attractiveness: category size and growth (users, spend per user); the shift to marketplaces and quick commerce (who owns the customer, channel fees); regulation and trust (FSSAI label rules, counterfeits).

keyMetrics.name: Money multiple for 25% IRR over 5 years
Required exit revenue
keyMetrics.formula: entry value x 3.05 / exit revenue multiple (ignoring debt and dilution)

keyMetrics.name: 12-month cohort retention
keyMetrics.formula: customers from a cohort still buying after 12 months / customers in the cohort

commonMistakes: Taking 55% growth at face value without splitting new from repeat revenue and checking cohort retention.
Assuming the exit multiple stays at 4.5x revenue, which hides how much future growth the entry price already assumes.

frameworkPick.why: It is an investment decision at a set price, so the tree follows due diligence (market, company, value creation, returns); the deciding issue is whether growth is repeatable, which needs a growth lens on cohorts and channels.

distractorWhyNot.ma: A financial buyer has no synergies or integration to test; the question is the return on a five-year hold at a set price, which due diligence logic answers.
distractorWhyNot.profitability: Negative EBITDA matters, but the question is price and return, not why margins fell.

cases.title: Marketplace buying a D2C brand
cases.prompt: Our client is a foreign-owned Indian online marketplace. It wants to buy a fast-growing D2C electronics accessories brand (₹600 crore revenue, 8% EBITDA) for about ₹2,400 crore, mainly to earn product margins instead of the commissions it now earns in that category. About 55% of the brand's sales happen on the client's own platform. Should it go ahead?
clarifyingFacts: Q: How is the client structured? A: It is majority foreign-owned and operates as a pure marketplace under India's FDI rules for e-commerce.
Q: Where does the brand sell? A: 55% on the client's marketplace, 25% on rival marketplaces, 12% on its own website, 8% in offline electronics stores.
Q: What are the margins? A: The brand's gross margin is 45%; the client earns about 18% commission plus 4% in advertising on the brand's sales.
Q: Is anyone else interested? A: A domestic consumer electronics company has also approached the founders.

modelTree.label: Should the client buy the accessories brand for about ₹2,400 crore?

children.label: Does the deal serve the strategic aim?
Product margin gained vs marketplace income lost
Brand margin on its on-platform sales
Commission and ads given up (about ₹73 crore a year)
Reaction of other sellers in the category
Trust in a platform that owns a competitor
Alternatives without ownership: exclusive launches, co-marketing
Is the brand worth ₹2,400 crore on its own?
Growth on rival platforms, website and offline
Marketing and returns cost per order
Price: 4x revenue, 50x EBITDA vs comparable deals
Is the deal allowed, and on what terms?
FDI rules: sellers with marketplace-group equity cannot sell on it
Revenue at risk if on-platform sales stop (₹330 crore)
Whether any compliant structure keeps the rationale
CCI: caught by ₹2,000 crore deal-value test despite small target
Scrutiny of platform neutrality and self-preferencing
Can value be kept after the deal?

hypotheses: Under India's FDI marketplace rules (Press Note 2 of 2018) a seller in which the marketplace group holds equity cannot sell on that marketplace, so after the deal about ₹330 crore of the brand's revenue is at risk and the client loses about ₹73 crore a year of commission and ads: the opposite of the intended margin gain.
Even without the FDI issue, ₹2,400 crore is 50x EBITDA and assumes the brand keeps a 55% dependence on one platform, which a rival bidder would not pay for.
An exclusive launch or co-marketing partnership captures some category economics without ownership and without alienating other sellers.
hints: Use the standard acquisition logic, but test the stated rationale with margin arithmetic before valuing anything.
First-level branches: does it serve the strategic aim; is the brand worth the price on its own; is the deal allowed; can value be kept after the deal.
Can value be kept after the deal: founder and team retention (earn-outs, lock-ins, brand autonomy); integration cost and timeline.

keyMetrics.name: Net annual gain from the deal
keyMetrics.formula: brand EBITDA kept after channel changes + synergies - commission and ad income given up - integration costs

keyMetrics.name: Implied multiples
keyMetrics.formula: ₹2,400 crore / ₹600 crore revenue = 4x; / ₹48 crore EBITDA = 50x

commonMistakes: Assuming the brand can keep selling on the client's platform after the deal, missing the FDI marketplace rules that defeat the main rationale.
Counting the brand's full margin as a gain without subtracting the commission and advertising income the client already earns from it.

frameworkPick.why: A strategic acquisition needs an M&A tree (rationale, standalone value, regulation, integration), and the rationale is a margin argument that must be tested with profitability logic: product margin gained against commission lost.

distractorWhyNot.market-entry: The client already operates in the category through its marketplace.
distractorWhyNot.pe-dd: The buyer is a strategic acquirer seeking synergies, not a financial investor planning an exit.

cases.title: Online furniture retailer running out of cash
cases.prompt: A European online furniture retailer with €380 million revenue sells mostly sofas and beds from its own stock. After a post-pandemic slump it has €55 million of cash and burns about €11 million a month, and its €80 million loan requires it to keep at least €25 million of cash at all times. The lenders want cash preserved; the founders want to keep spending on marketing to return to growth. What should the company do?
clarifyingFacts: Q: Where is the cash going? A: An operating loss of about €4 million a month, plus about €7 million a month of stock bought for the autumn peak that has not yet sold. Capital spending is small.
Q: What does inventory look like? A: €140 million of stock, about 40% of it older than nine months; suppliers are paid on 30-day terms on average.

Q: What are the unit economics? A: Gross margin 42%; two-person delivery and returns cost about 18% of revenue; marketing is 14% of revenue, with new customers taking over 18 months to pay back their acquisition cost.
Q: What support is available? A: The lenders will consider a covenant waiver in return for a 13-week cash plan; shareholders might provide a bridge loan if the plan is credible.

modelTree.label: How can the retailer stay above its €25m cash floor and return to viability?

children.label: Reduce the operating loss (about €4m a month)
Cut delivery and returns cost (18% of revenue)
Keep only marketing that pays back
Pause channels whose payback is longer than the cash runway
Shift spend to repeat and referral customers
Resize fixed costs to the smaller business
Sell aged stock (about €56m over nine months old)
Cancel or delay unsold peak-season orders
Extend supplier payment terms beyond 30 days
Lenders: waiver or reset of the covenant
Fees or higher interest as the price
Amount needed to fund the plan

hypotheses: Working capital is the fastest lever: stopping the €7m monthly stock build alone cuts burn to about €4m and stretches headroom from 2.7 to about 7.5 months, and clearing part of the €56m of aged stock buys more.

Marketing (about €4.4m a month) is what lenders and founders disagree on; with average payback over 18 months and under three months of headroom, almost none of it returns cash in time, so a rule of funding only channels that pay back within the plan period (mostly repeat and referral) settles which spend continues.
Delivery and returns at 18% of revenue point to high damage and failed-delivery rates that can be cut within a quarter.
hints: Build the tree from the cash equation rather than the profit equation.
First-level branches: reduce the operating loss; release cash from working capital; cut capital spending; secure funding and covenant headroom.
Secure funding and covenant headroom: lenders' waiver or reset (13-week cash plan, weekly reporting, fees); shareholder bridge (amount needed, milestones for each tranche).

keyMetrics.name: Months until covenant breach
keyMetrics.formula: (cash - €25m floor) / monthly net burn = (€55m - €25m) / €11m ≈ 2.7 months

keyMetrics.name: Monthly net burn
keyMetrics.formula: operating loss + increase in working capital + capital spending - new funding

commonMistakes: Proposing a long-term growth or cost programme without first fixing the 13-week cash position, when the covenant breaks in under three months.
Taking one side in the lender-founder conflict instead of using marketing payback to decide which spend continues.

frameworkPick.why: A cash crunch with a covenant about to break calls for a turnaround tree built on the cash equation, and most of the levers (stock, delivery, returns) are operational.

distractorWhyNot.profitability: Losses matter, but the binding constraint is cash and the covenant, which a profit tree misses (working capital, funding).
distractorWhyNot.growth: Returning to growth is the founders' wish, but the company cannot fund it until it survives the next quarter.

Dark store, rider, packaging and payment costs
options.why: Overlap: wastage is already netted in product margin, so write-offs of expired and damaged stock are counted twice.

split: Product margin after discounts and wastage
options.why: Covers every revenue line and every per-order cost once: product margin, fees and ads, less variable costs.

split: Product margin after discounts and wastage
Central tech and category team costs
options.why: Not a driver: central teams are fixed overheads that sit below contribution and do not change with each order.

quick.question: Which split of 'Lifetime value (LTV) of a D2C customer' is MECE?
quick.parent: Lifetime value (LTV) of a D2C customer

options.why: Wrong quantity: these multiply to lifetime revenue, not value; product, shipping and returns costs are missing.
LTV = contribution per order x orders per year x years active; the three factors multiply to lifetime contribution and none is counted twice.
Overlap: repeat rate is already captured by orders per year and years active, so adding it double counts retention.
Not a driver: CAC is what LTV is compared with (the LTV/CAC ratio); it is spent before the customer's lifetime and does not change what the customer is worth afterwards.

chainDrills.prompt: A D2C brand's customer complaints about damaged products tripled and its returns cost rose. Courier transit times and handling scores are unchanged; the rise began the week the warehouse switched to a thinner, cheaper mailer box. In which stage is the cause?
chainDrills.why: The cost shows up in returns (s6) and looks like transit damage (s5), but courier handling is unchanged; packaging is chosen and applied at pick-pack in the warehouse (s4), so that is where the fix lies.

chainDrills.prompt: Put the stages of the e-commerce value chain in order, from making the product to keeping the customer.
chainDrills.why: The product is made, demand is created, the customer orders on a storefront, the order is picked and packed, shipped and delivered, and finally returns, service and retention decide whether the customer buys again.

chainDrills.prompt: A brand's prepaid sales are settled within two days, but cash from COD orders takes 10-15 days to reach its bank account, straining working capital. Where does this delay sit?
chainDrills.why: COD cash is collected by the delivery partner at the door and remitted later, which is part of shipping and last-mile delivery. Prepaid settlement through the gateway happens at the storefront and is not the problem.

chainDrills.prompt: Assign each cost to the stage where it is incurred: inbound freight from the contract manufacturer; fee paid to an affiliate site for each order it refers; commission paid to a marketplace; packaging material for each parcel; COD collection fee charged by the courier; reverse pickup for a size exchange.

items.item: Inbound freight from the contract manufacturer to the warehouse
Fee paid to an affiliate site for each order it refers
COD collection fee charged by the courier
Reverse pickup for a size exchange

chainDrills.why: Inbound freight is part of getting the product to the brand (s1), not customer delivery. An affiliate fee is paid per order like a commission, but it buys traffic, so it is demand generation (s2); marketplace commission is the price of someone else's storefront (s3). Packaging is applied at pick-pack (s4). The COD fee looks like a payment cost, but cash collection is done by the courier at the door (s5). A reverse pickup belongs to returns (s6) even when the same courier does it, because the return causes the cost.

chainDrills.prompt: During a sale, website checkout conversion fell from 3.1% to 2.4%. Traffic quality and prices were unchanged, but the site showed delivery dates six days out instead of two because the fulfilment centre had a three-day picking backlog. Which stage caused the fall?
chainDrills.why: The symptom appears at the storefront (s3), but the cause is the fulfilment centre's backlog (s4), which pushed out the delivery promise. Fixing site design or ads would not help.

chainDrills.prompt: A D2C brand's RTO rate rose from 12% to 22% in a quarter, while website conversion rose 15%. Ad audiences, spend and prices are unchanged, and courier first-attempt delivery rates and address quality are normal. The change began when the brand dropped OTP verification for COD orders at checkout to make buying faster. Where is the root cause?
chainDrills.why: The cost shows up in shipping and returns (s5, s6), and a falling-quality audience (s2) is the usual suspect, but traffic is unchanged. Removing OTP checks at checkout (s3) let impulsive and fake COD orders through, which is also why conversion rose at the same time; restoring verification for COD fixes it.
